Why Margaret Atwood gave the best advice on "The Gardian Ten rules for writing fiction " ?

Margaret Atwood

1 Take a pencil to write with on aeroplanes. Pens leak. But if the pencil breaks, you can't sharpen it on the plane, because you can't take knives with you. Therefore: take two pencils.

2 If both pencils break, you can do a rough sharpening job with a nail file of the metal or glass type.

3 Take something to write on. Paper is good. In a pinch, pieces of wood or your arm will do.

4 If you're using a computer, always safeguard new text with a ­memory stick.

5 Do back exercises. Pain is distracting.

6 Hold the reader's attention. (This is likely to work better if you can hold your own.) But you don't know who the reader is, so it's like shooting fish with a slingshot in the dark. What ­fascinates A will bore the pants off B.

7 You most likely need a thesaurus, a rudimentary grammar book, and a grip on reality. This latter means: there's no free lunch. Writing is work. It's also gambling. You don't get a pension plan. Other people can help you a bit, but ­essentially you're on your own. ­Nobody is making you do this: you chose it, so don't whine.

8 You can never read your own book with the innocent anticipation that comes with that first delicious page of a new book, because you wrote the thing. You've been backstage. You've seen how the rabbits were smuggled into the hat. Therefore ask a reading friend or two to look at it before you give it to anyone in the publishing business. This friend should not be someone with whom you have a ­romantic relationship, unless you want to break up.

9 Don't sit down in the middle of the woods. If you're lost in the plot or blocked, retrace your steps to where you went wrong. Then take the other road. And/or change the person. Change the tense. Change the opening page.

10 Prayer might work. Or reading ­something else. Or a constant visual­isation of the holy grail that is the finished, published version of your resplendent book.

No cliche (write every day, 2nd draft=1st draft -10%, etc..), very specific, self referential humor...

I actually think Amazon and eBay have gone a little too far, in terms of preventing third-party merchants from selling Confederate flags. I'm fine with businesses that choose not to sell them, but to be an outlet for other businesses to sell merchandise and dictate what legal items they can and cannot sell, sort of crosses the line for me. If Amazon and eBay feel that they need to control legal products sold through their web site, then they should not allow third-party merchants to sell any products at all. Wal-Mart and Sears have never allowed third-party merchants to sell through their stores, so I have no problem with their decision in this matter.

Sears has third party merchants selling through their website.

The Amazon marketplace has all kinds of rules in place for third party sellers. Entire product categories are off limits for sellers. Sellers have been restricted from selling specific products that they were previously allowed to sell (Disney Frozen).

I was unaware that Sears allowed third-party merchants to sell through their website. When I spoke of them, I had only been thinking about their brick-and-mortar stores, as well. But if this is the case that they allow third-party merchants to sell online, then I stand by my opinion that they should not restrict Confederate flags from being sold in this capacity. I also disagree with any restrictions that Amazon places upon its third-party merchants, which I feel defeats the entire purpose of allowing citizens to use it as a platform for business. If Amazon wishes to deny shipping on behalf of merchants who sell products that do not align with their policies, I would absolutely support Amazon's decision in this regard. However, people should be allowed to market and ship what they wish, provided that it is within the confines of the law, and sellers are willing to take full responsibility for seeing that it reaches the consumer.
